passages.happening:
“Then Moses assembled the whole congregation of Israel and said to them, ‘These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do: For six days work may be done, but the seventh day shall be your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD’” (verses 1-2).

“Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The covenant has been renewed. The plans Moses received in chapters 25 to 31 can at last be carried out. Chapters 35 to 40 tell how the tabernacle was built, and they repeat those plans closely, now as things done.

Notice where Moses begins. The plans ended with the Sabbath (31:12-17). The building begins with it. Before a single gift is brought or a single board cut, the people are told when to stop. Even the work of making God's house does not override the day of rest.

The penalty in verse 2 is the same as in chapter 31, and the note there faces it. It was the law of Israel as a nation under God, it is no pattern for anyone today, and no Christian tradition applies it.

Verse 3 is new. No fire is to be lit in any home on the Sabbath. In the wilderness, lighting a fire meant gathering fuel and doing real work. The verse shaped later Jewish practice. The rabbis understood it to forbid lighting a fire on the Sabbath, but not having one already lit, so Sabbath lamps are lit before sundown. Karaite Jews historically read it more strictly and kept no fire burning at all.
passages.later:
The Sabbath had first been given with the manna: “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (Exodus 16:23).

Luke notes that the women who followed Jesus, with his body in the tomb and spices to prepare, “rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment” (Luke 23:56).

Christians differ on how the Sabbath applies to them. The notes on Exodus 16 and 31 set out the views, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: The first word to a forgiven people at work was a word about rest. Ask whether you treat even your work for God as too urgent to stop. And ask what it would look like to begin a great task by settling when you will rest.

passages.t: A call for gifts and for skill
passages.happening:
“Take from among you an offering to the LORD. Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD: gold, silver, and bronze” (verse 5), with yarn, linen, goat hair, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices and gemstones (verses 6-9).

“Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded” (verse 10). Then Moses lists it all: the tabernacle and its frames, the ark and the veil, the table, the lampstand, the two altars, the basin, the courtyard, the tent pegs and the priests' garments (verses 11-19).
passages.hearers:
Moses passes on what God told him in 25:1-9. Two things are asked of the people: what they have, and what they can do.

The gift is to come from ‘everyone whose heart is willing’. It is not a tax. No amount is set. The Hebrew word for the offering, terumah, comes from a verb meaning to lift up: something lifted out of what a person owns and set apart for God.

The list of things to be made runs quickly through chapters 25 to 30. The notes on those chapters describe each one: the ark and its mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the basin and the garments.

Stories of temple building from elsewhere in the ancient world follow a familiar order: a god's command and plan, the gathering of materials and workers, the building, and the dedication. Gudea, a ruler in southern Mesopotamia about 2100 BC, left inscriptions telling how he received a temple plan in a dream and built it with care. Exodus follows the same broad order, with one sharp difference. The builders here are not a king's forced laborers. They are a whole people, giving and working because they want to.

That would not have been lost on the first hearers. These people had built for Pharaoh as slaves.
passages.later:
When David gathered gifts for the temple, “the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders, for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly” (1 Chronicles 29:9). David prayed, “everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

Paul asks the same kind of gift from the church: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.asks: God asked for gifts from willing hearts, and for the work of skilled hands. Ask what you have that God could use, and what you can do. And ask whether you give because you must, or because your heart is willing.

passages.t: Men and women bring what they have
passages.happening:
“And everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD for the work on the Tent of Meeting” (verse 21).

“So all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry” (verse 22). Others bring yarn, linen, skins, silver, bronze and wood (verses 23-24).

“Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun” (verse 25). “And all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair” (verse 26). The leaders bring gemstones, spices and oil (verses 27-28).

“So all the men and women of the Israelites whose hearts prompted them brought a freewill offering to the LORD” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Set this scene beside chapter 32. There the people took the gold from their ears for a god they could see. Here they bring their earrings again, freely, for the God who has forgiven them. The same people, the same kind of gold, and a different heart.

The word ‘heart’ runs all through the chapter. In Hebrew the heart is the center of a person's will and thought, not only of feeling. Hearts are willing, stirred and prompted. A ‘freewill offering’ was a gift beyond anything the law required.

The text names women again and again (verses 22, 25, 26 and 29). Spinning yarn and goat hair was the skilled work of women in an ancient household. The chapter counts it as part of the holy task, beside metalwork and carving. The same Hebrew word for wisdom is used of the craftsmen and of the women who spin.

Everyone brings something different. Some have gold. Some have goat hair. Some have only the skill of their hands. Leaders and ordinary people, men and women, build God's dwelling together, and every gift is needed.

The gold is presented as a ‘wave offering’. The giver lifted or moved the gift before the LORD to hand it over to him.
passages.later:
Luke says of the women who traveled with Jesus, “These women were ministering to them out of their own means” (Luke 8:3).

Paul pictures the church as a body that “grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part” (Ephesians 4:16), and Peter writes, “each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10).

Jesus honored the smallest gift of all. Of a poor widow's two small coins he said, “this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury” (Mark 12:43).
passages.asks: The gold that once made a calf was now given freely for God's house. Ask what you once gave to the wrong thing that you could now give to God. And ask whose quiet, skilled work in your church goes unnoticed, as the spinning might have.

passages.t: Bezalel and Oholiab, able to teach
passages.happening:
“Then Moses said to the Israelites, ‘See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship’” (verses 30-31).

“And the LORD has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the ability to teach others” (verse 34). They are skilled as engravers, designers, embroiderers and weavers (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Moses tells the people what God told him in 31:1-6, almost word for word. The note on chapter 31 says more about Bezalel, about the Spirit's gift of skill, and about the tribes of Judah and Dan.

One thing is added here. God has given both men ‘the ability to teach others’. The Hebrew verb for teaching shares a root with torah, the word for God's instruction. The skill God gives is not kept by two gifted men. It is passed on. The Spirit's gifts spread through the people.

So the work is shared from the start. Two men are named, and many are trained.
passages.later:
Paul gives Timothy the same charge about the faith itself: “entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2).

He describes the church as a building still going up: “in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22).
passages.hard:
Why does Exodus repeat the tabernacle plans almost word for word?

Many readers find chapters 35 to 40 slow, since so much repeats chapters 25 to 31. Several reasons work together.

Repeating was normal in ancient writing, and above all in accounts of building. The command and the doing were both written down, to show that the work was done just as ordered. In an age when books were read aloud, repetition also helped the memory.

After the golden calf, the repeating carries weight of its own. The people who made an image to their own design now build God's dwelling exactly to his design, and the text wants the reader to see the two match. Command followed by exact obedience is what a restored relationship looks like on the page.

Scholars also note that the old Greek translation arranges these last chapters in a different order from the Hebrew. That suggests they were passed down in more than one form before the text settled.
passages.asks: God gave Bezalel skill, and the ability to teach it. Ask what you know how to do that you could teach someone else. And ask who taught you, and whether you have thanked God for them.
